Thank you very much. I thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo for the invitation to brief today's ARIA Formula meeting. The International Crisis Group is a global conflict prevention organization mandated to support peaceful efforts towards preventing, mitigating, and resolving conflicts. In addition to our on-the-ground research, we are developing a new database tool for monitoring mining and critical infrastructure in conflict-affected regions. In many of the cases we follow closely, we see linkages between natural resource and deadly violence. In Myanmar, control of northern Kachin State's jade economy has become one of the major stakes in the conflict between the military and the Tachin Independence Organization. In the Great Lakes region, the M23 insurgency captured the Coltan Beach Mabaya mining site in April 2024, obtaining a predictable and significant source of revenue and allowing the rebels to enrich themselves in northern Kivu Province. In the Amazon Basin, Brazilian organized crime Colombian armed groups like the ELN and Secunda Marquetela have fanned out across borders in search of gold mines and trafficking routes. Demonstrative of the scale of illicit economies at stake, just one group in Ecuador, Los Choneros, reportedly earned some $1 million monthly from illegal gold. These linkages should not come as a surprise. States and non-state armed groups are now locked in intense competition to control natural resources and their supply chains, not only for material wealth but also as part of their broader geopolitical calculations. Competition over critical minerals is especially intense. These minerals are embedded in supply chains across the world and are essential to our global economy. Some resources are commonplace in the household goods while others are integral to clean energy technology, rapid expansion of AI infrastructure, or increasingly advanced defense systems. This competition has profound consequences for countries affected by armed conflict, many of which are themselves major reserves of the natural resources that drive this global trade. Compounding this challenge is the growing gap between international norms and practice. Existing policies on environmental standards, natural resource management, and supply chain responsibility treat the intersection of conflict and natural resources as an issue that can be managed through localized technical fixes, but they often fail to consider the regional and international dynamics that shape the competition over natural resources in conflict-affected settings. These weaknesses of current approaches are also evident in the Security Council's portfolio on the subject. Previous resolutions and statements by this body have touched on parts of the broader nexus between conflict minerals and natural resource exploitation. These have included most notably the 2003 Council resolution endorsing the Kimberley Process certification scheme and the 2019 Council resolution on silencing the guns in Africa. But political follow-up from governments remains thin on the ground, and the Council has yet to consider a more holistic approach to this issue. Indeed, most of the Council's current reporting on this issue is channeled through its subsidiary bodies and panels of experts. In the hope of stimulating your discussions, I would like to offer 4 observations on the links between conflict and natural resources. First, natural resources are rarely the root causes of conflict, but they, but they do shape its trajectory. In many of the areas of concern, wars are the products of political struggles over power, identity, and autonomy. Elsewhere, criminal groups that now exploit these resources often rose to prominence through other illicit activities, particularly drug trafficking. Control of natural resources and critical minerals has become an important source of finance, leverage, and military advantage for conflict parties and organized crimes. For example, gold trafficking provides criminal networks in the Amazon Basin with the money they need to corrupt state officials, with criminal spending often exceeding the budgets of law enforcement agencies tasked with combating them. Secondly, the changing political— the changing geopolitical environment exacerbates how global dependence on critical minerals adds more pressure onto fragile conflict zones. In the eastern DRC, there is abundant evidence that foreign powers and the armed groups they support are smuggling out as much of the region's mineral resources and wealth. Their connections to global markets only reinforces the region's persistent cycles of conflict despite frequent peace agreements. This dynamic also works in the opposite direction. Actions taken in one remote area of the world can have global ramifications. For example, a 2023 decision by the United Wa State Army in Myanmar to suspend its mining of tin ore, a critical component of semiconductors used in servers and AI data centers, raised global prices by nearly 12% overnight. Thirdly, efforts to bring peace need to address the way revenues from natural resources are distributed alongside political and security questions. Time and again, extraction of mineral wealth has led to very few social or economic benefits for citizens and communities, including the many who depend on artisanal and small-scale mining. The pattern holds even in areas unaffected by armed group violence. External predation is the primary driver of why mineral wealth does not reach ordinary citizens, so sustainable paths to peace need to consider the ways these resource supply chains are governed and who benefits. And fourthly, the political cost of weak resource governance are both domestic and cross-border, particularly in environment— in environmental terms. This is nowhere more evident than in the 9 countries where territory in the Amazon Basin, the world's largest tropical rainforest. Illegal mining and gold trafficking contaminate waterways that cross frontiers, harming soil and plant life, while timber extraction and deforestation risk transforming the Amazon from a global carbon sink to a carbon resource. So what to do? We believe that the goal for all states should be to build comprehensive approaches to natural resource management that reduce incentives for violence, improve accountability, and ensure that natural resource wealth benefits communities contributing to and living alongside all parts of these supply chains. Internationally, we see a role for more active engagement from the United Nations. Formal and informal council sessions like today's can gradually help build consensus around the link between natural resource exploitation and conflict, even if that link is complex and context-specific. Member states and private corporations alike should draw upon an array of technical expertise such as those outlined in the UN guidance on critical energy transition minerals to make sure their due diligence, risk management, and human rights practices are sharp and up to date. But these practices cannot be seen as box-checking measures. They will need to be accompanied by detailed ground-level information and political analysis to understand both the short and long-term conflict risks, particularly considering the gold rush from critical supply chains. In some instances, UN peacekeeping missions and political offices operating in these areas can be useful ports of call. In others, experts in UN country teams may be better positioned to bridge those gaps. In the long run, Member states should take steps to improve how they cooperate on natural resources to reduce the frictions that are becoming more common in this era of strategic competition. That is especially true regarding critical minerals. According to a UN 2025 study conducted by UN Working Group on Extractive Industries and Sustainable Development, there are 150 and/or regional initiatives, partnerships, or alliances on critical energy transition minerals. There is no established global forum to promote dialogue and cooperation among all the stakeholders involved in the sector, even as critical mineral chains risk fragmenting along geopolitical lines. The surge in geopolitical interest across critical minerals provides an opening to create a platform for deconfliction. We hope that tomorrow's high-level meeting on critical energy transitions minerals and the 22nd June Security Council open debate on natural resource governance are chances to start that process, and this area certainly lays the groundwork. I thank you for your attention.

Excellencies, Ministers, distinguished delegates, thank you for the opportunity to speak today. It is particularly meaningful to discuss this issue in a forum convened by the Democratic Republic of Congo, a country that sits at the heart of the global conversation on critical minerals. I'm the director of the Critical Minerals Security Program at CSIS. We are an independent Washington think tank, and I'm American, but I began my career in South Africa's Platinum Belt 13 years ago, shortly after the Marikana massacre, which was the deadliest use of force by South African security forces against civilians in nearly 4 decades. Since then, I've spent my career working on critical minerals across Africa. I've met government leaders, miners, investors, and local communities who see mining as both— with both hope and apprehension. And it's taught me something I've carried through my career, which is that the same mineral wealth can be a source of conflict, or it can be an incredible catalyst for development. And the difference isn't geology, it's governance. So our challenge is not simply to produce more minerals, which can sometimes be the rhetoric coming out of the Global North, but it's how to govern them in a way that strengthens stability rather than fuels instability, generates prosperity rather than deepens inequality, and reinforces international cooperation rather than geopolitical fragmentation. Now, I think, you know, there's a, there's an old British comedian, he said there's no such thing as new news, it's old news happening to new people. So I think there's something to take to that, is when you look at the history of the DRC, it offers a really powerful lesson. Following independence, the secession of Katanga demonstrated how strategic mineral wealth could become deeply intertwined with political contestation, with foreign interests and conflict. 20 years ago, I was reading a report that said Katanga was widely viewed as a symbol of instability. But today we know that the copper-cobalt belt of southeastern DRC is comparatively stable and one of Africa's most important destinations for large-scale mining investment and a critical source of minerals for the global economy. The DRC today produces roughly 70% of the world's cobalt and the world's second largest producer of copper in the same region that was once identified as a symbol of instability. The transformation illustrates a very central point. Stability is not static, and it can be built through stronger institutions, improved governance, sustained investment, and partnerships that create benefits for local communities. Katanga shows us that instability is not permanent and that with governance, mining can be a force for good. Now, when we look at— when we step back and we look at the nexus between natural resources governance and international security, The surge in the demand for critical minerals has fundamentally changed the relationship between natural resources and international peace. For decades, natural resource governance was largely viewed as a development issue. Today, it's increasingly being viewed as a strategic imperative. Critical minerals underpin the technologies that will shape the 21st century, from clean energy and artificial intelligence to defense systems and advanced manufacturing. As a result, the quality of governance no longer affects only domestic prosperity, but global economic resilience and international security. Resource wealth is not destiny. Countries with similar geological endowments have experienced remarkably different outcomes. Transparent institutions, predictable regulatory frameworks, and accountable management of mineral revenues are not simply good policy, They are the foundations for lasting peace and stability. The shift also requires us to rethink how we think about supply chain resilience. Too often, resilience is viewed solely through the lens of importing countries seeking to secure access to minerals. But resilient supply chains begin in producing countries. They depend on the governments that provide that policy certainty, communities that share the benefits of that resource development, and investors who have confidence that projects will be supported over decades and not election cycles. When communities see mining as a source of development rather than extraction, trust grows. When governments manage resource wealth transparently and responsibly, public confidence grows. And when, and when investors operate under clear and predictable rules, long-term capital flows. Those outcomes reinforce one another, creating a virtuous cycle in which economic development and peace become mutually reinforcing rather than competing objectives. It's important to remember that peace is not just a humanitarian objective, it's an economic prerequisite. Long-term investment follows stability, and stability is strengthened when citizens see tangible benefits from their natural resources. So ultimately, the question before us is not simply how the world secures the minerals it needs. It is whether the growing demand for critical minerals becomes an opportunity to build those stronger institutions, more resilient economies, and deeper international partnerships. Now, the international community has developed norms around conflict minerals, but what we do also need is norms around responsible partnerships, because partnerships have become the central discussion of the last 2 years. I know that sitting in Washington. Countries have followed different paths, but the most successful examples share common characteristics when it comes to partnerships. Governance is transparent. There is long-term investment in both people and infrastructure. If you go to Katanga, you see how much energy infrastructure has been built through strategic partnerships, and a commitment to capturing value through skills processing and technology transfer. Now, these ambitions shouldn't be viewed as being at tension— in tension with investment. In fact, they can reinforce it. Mining is amongst the most capital-intensive industries in the world, and developing a large-scale mine requires billions of dollars, often more than a decade before production begins. Investors therefore require that stability, and producer countries meanwhile have a very legitimate expectation that the development of these resources will generate lasting economic benefits. So achieving this balance requires genuine partnership, and governments can create that stability. Development finance institutions reduce investment risk. Multilateral institutions strengthen governance and transparency. And each has a distinct role, but none can succeed alone. These partnerships can only support responsible mining— not only support responsible mining, but the infrastructure, the workforce, the geological knowledge and data, the environmental stewardship, and commercially viable opportunities. So this is not a challenge that any one country, company, or institution can solve alone. It requires a shared commitment to partnership, transparency, and mutual benefit. So as the international community considers future action, I believe our, our approach should rest on 4 principles. First, sovereignty over natural resource and international partnership should be viewed as complementary rather than as competing principles. Every nation has the sovereign right to determine how its resources are developed, consistent with international law, exercised through transparent governance, accountable institutions, and predictable policy frameworks, that sovereignty becomes a foundation for investment, development, and international cooperation. Strong institutions are the most effective safeguards against corruption, public distrust, and investor uncertainty. Second, investment frameworks must balance commercial competitiveness with long-term public benefit. Durable partnerships require both financial viability and broad societal legitimacy. Third, sustainability must be understood more broadly than maybe we think about it. Long-term success requires balancing environmental responsibility to ensure that communities are not bearing the benefits of these operations, the interests of those local communities, and economic competitiveness. It will be no exaggeration to state I would like to say that the topic that has been selected is exceedingly sensitive for virtually all states insofar as it touches upon matters of sovereignty and, on the whole, matter of the future that each country can count on. The Russian Federation shares the view that effective natural resource management is designed to facilitate sustainable development, to strengthen statehood, and to reduce the risks of conflicts reemerging. And this is precisely the approach that we are guided by in considering this issue during— at specialized platforms. And at the same time, we firmly believe that the Security Council should not discuss general approaches in this sphere. On the contrary, the Security Council should focus its attention on country-specific and region-specific situations. Today, we believe it is necessary to note the following. First and foremost, it would be erroneous to regard natural resources as the root cause of conflicts that break out. Conflicts break out not owing to the presence or the absence of natural resources, but as a consequence of political instability, weak state institutions, terrorist activity, as well as other factors which include the increasingly blatant— with echoes of the Middle Ages— manifestation of the factor of external intervention in domestic affairs of sovereign states. It is indeed the desire of certain elites to establish control over the natural wealth of others States, which lies at the heart of and is the reason behind many and most conflicts. This is frequently becoming the engine for the aggressive policies which for decades have been embraced by former colonialist powers using various pretexts, either be it exporting democracy or protecting human rights. Or other lofty political slogans, these parties seek to achieve parochial agendas and goals of ensuring unfettered access to natural wealth. And in fact, this is an egregious manifestation of neocolonialism. Recent history probably indeed abounds with a number of such examples. Let us touch upon the neocolonialist approaches of which have been fueling numerous conflicts on the African continent, including in Mali, Niger, and South Sudan. And this is also borne out by the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Struggles over access to strategically important Congolese minerals is one of the causes for the protracted crisis in that country. Control over extraction and illicit trade—
Thank you.

of coltan, cobalt, copper, gold, diamonds is something which not only armed groups are competing over, but also state actors are competing over this. And a particular role in these processes is played by extra-regional economic interests. Attempts to resolve the conflict in the east of the DRC will be futile if countries of the Great Lakes region failed to adopt resolute coordinated measures to combat illicit exploitation and the trafficking in natural resources. More than ever before, it is necessary for there to be regional efforts to unify mineral certification mechanisms and for supply chain governance. Any international standards in this area need to be crafted purely on the basis of broad international consensus. They need to be non-discriminatory in nature They need to take into account the national specificities of states, and they must not generate new obstacles for their socioeconomic development. The priority here needs to be on duly taking into account the interests of developing producing states, and this is inextricably linked to the provision of technical support, advanced technology transfer, including at preferential and on preferential and concessionary conditions. As well as enhancing financial support volumes to enhance the processing capabilities and technological sovereignty of extractive countries. These kinds of approaches are completely incompatible with the imposition of unilateral coercive measures, which undermine the investment appeal of states. They destroy. Disrupt supply chains and they obstruct the development of a processing industry. They hamper access to technologies and significantly complicate post-conflict recovery. In connection with the above, we are not in a position to agree with the premise about the existence of some kind of a normative gap in international governance of matters of natural resources in the context of armed conflicts. This is not where the problem lies. The problem lies in the deliberate maintenance of hotspots of instability by those who gain political and economic advantages from this. It is equally important to bear in mind that the principle of the sovereignty of states over their natural resources constitutes one of the fundamental principles of of international law. Today, unfortunately, we have heard a great deal of concessions and qualifications being made when it comes to the principle of sovereignty. Any international initiatives, including the ideas that have been heard about traceability, need to be conducted in accordance with the principle of sovereignty. And they mustn't establish mechanisms which limit the legitimate right of states to do independently determined procedures for the extraction, use, and processing of their own resources. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation, and I now give the floor to the representative of the United States, to be followed by Somalia and Pakistan.

Thank you, Ambassador. And I'd also like to thank the Democratic Republic of the Congo for convening this important meeting as part of its July Security Council presidency. And Foreign Minister, your presence here today is a testament to the vital and timely nature of this topic. As President Trump has said, America's foreign policy has 2 main goals: to ensure prosperity at home and to ensure peace abroad. A diverse and reliable supply of critical minerals, supported by a secure and resilient global supply chain, is essential to both of these goals. The United States and our partners have a shared interest in diversifying supply chains and avoiding overreliance on any single country for critical minerals and other essential materials. Open markets strengthen the global economy and reduce the risk of conflict. It is with this goal in mind the United States brought together like-minded countries for a ministerial meeting in Washington in February to take decisive action. Together, we launched the new Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement, or FORGE. FORGE partners will collaborate at the policy and project levels to advance initiatives that strengthen diversified, resilient critical mineral value chains. The United States is also mobilizing unprecedented resources to secure critical mineral supply chains supporting projects with more than $30 billion in letters of interest, investments, loans, and other support over the past months in partnership with the private sector. Reliable and sustainable access is vital not only to our collective prosperity but also to regional and global security. It will reduce strategic vulnerabilities, ensure no nation is left unduly dependent, and deny adversaries opportune— opportunities to exploit critical We see the challenges firsthand in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where illicit exploitation of natural resources enables violence against and exploitation of the Congolese people. That is why the United States took decisive action last month against Rwandan individuals and mining companies for their connections to illegal mineral trafficking. Our sanctions aim to compel compliance with the historic U.S.-brokered Washington Accords and reinforce our commitment to implement the Regional Economic Integration Framework. The Regional Economic Integration Framework is designed to expand trade and investment, strengthen transparency across critical mineral supply chains, and lay the foundation for greater long-term economic opportunity throughout the region. The United States remains prepared to use all tools at its disposal to promote peace in eastern DRC. From his first day in office, President Trump has made it clear that economic security is national security. Together, we can strengthen trusted partnerships, diversify critical mineral value chains, and ensure our economies prosper free from coercion, disruption, or violence. Thank you.
I thank the United States, and I now give the floor to Somalia, to be followed by Pakistan and Latvia.

Madam President, at the outset, allow me to thank the Democratic Republic of Congo for convening this timely Africa Area Formula meeting on the nexus between natural resources, conflict, and peacebuilding. We are also pleased to welcome Her Excellence, Ms. Theresa Wagner, the Foreign Minister of the Democratic Republic of Congo, whose presence underscores the importance attached to this important discussion. We also thank the briefers for their valuable insights. Natural resources occupy a unique place in today's global landscape. They are indispensable to the energy transition, technological innovation, and economic growth. At the same time, where governance gaps exist, illicit exploitation and trafficking can fuel armed groups, undermine state authority, and prolong the conflict. The challenge before us is therefore not the existence of natural resources themselves, but ensuring that they are governed in a manner that promotes peace, security, and sustainable development. Allow me to make 3 points. First, while the conflict dimension is critical, African perspective equally underscores the importance of natural minerals, our strategic assets for development, industrialization, and shared prosperity. For many African countries, critical minerals and other natural resources represent an opportunity to accelerate structural transformation, create employment, and advance implementation of the Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals. In this regard, the African Mining Vision provides an important continental framework by promoting the transparent, equitable, and optimal exploitation of African mineral resources while emphasizing local value addition. Beneficiation, industrial development, and regional integration. Any future discussion on natural resources and peace should therefore strike an appropriate balance between addressing security risks and enabling producing countries to derive sustainable and equitable benefits from their natural wealth. Second, strengthening governance should remain the cornerstone of our collective efforts. Existing due diligence, transparency, and traceability initiatives have made important contributions toward responsible resource management. However, these efforts should be accompanied by a sustained investment in the national capacities, institutional strengthening, and technical assistance. Responsible governance cannot be achieved through standards alone. It also requires capable national institutions, effective border management, transparent regulatory frameworks, and international partnerships that empower producing countries rather than impose disproportionate compliance burdens upon them. Third, Somalia supports the continued discussion towards a more coherent and comprehensive international framework addressing the relationship between natural resources and peace. Such efforts should build upon existing mechanisms, avoid duplication, and fully respect national sovereignty and ownership. The Security Council has an important role where the illicit exploitation and trafficking of natural resources contribute to the threats to international peace and security. Its efforts should complement the work of the relevant regional organizations and international institutions, while taking into account the different circumstances and priorities of producing countries. In this regard, regional frameworks, including African Mining Vision, provide valuable guidance on promoting responsible resource governance that advances peace, sustainable development and shared prosperity. Madam President, natural resources, wherever they are found, should serve as a foundation for peace, shared prosperity and sustainable development, rather than a driver of conflict and instability. Achieving these objectives requires genuine partnership, shared responsibility, transparent governance, equitable benefit sharing and greater value addition to producing countries, including across Africa, so that the benefits of natural resources contribute to the long-term peace and inclusive development. Somalia remains committed to engaging constructively in these discussions and to supporting nationally owned and internationally coordinated approach to a responsible natural resource governance. I thank you.
I thank Somalia, and I now give the floor to Pakistan, who will be followed by Latvia and Colombia.

We thank you, Madam Foreign Minister, for convening and chairing this very important Aria Formula meeting, and we also thank the briefers for their invaluable insights. Natural resources should serve as instruments of sustainable development, shared prosperity, and peace, and not coercion, conflict, or geopolitical competition. As we have heard in this meeting, Pakistan has long stood in solidarity with African countries in their pursuit of sovereign control over their natural wealth and development. Africa's experience shows that where mineral wealth intersects with weak governance, illicit exploitation, and external interference, the risks of instability increase. And historically, there has always been a contest for resources, and we know that when resources are scarce, there is a scramble for those resources. And in recent times, the growing demand for critical minerals driven by the energy transition Digital transformation and advanced manufacturing has created new geopolitical and geo-economic pressures, and if not managed responsibly, competition over strategic natural resources can create new risks and vulnerabilities for international peace and security. And this, Madam President, also applies. Equally to water, the most vital natural resource for humankind, shared water resources are essential for life, sustainable development, and regional stability. Unfortunately, today we are faced with a very grave situation in our own region where our neighbors India has sought to weaponize water against Pakistan. We are deeply concerned by these developments and reject India's unilateral and unlawful action to put the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, which is a violation of international law and treaty's own provisions. The international community must urge India to return to full compliance with the treaty, which remains valid and in force as affirmed by the August 2025 award of the Court of Arbitration. Madam President, Pakistan believes that the governance of natural resources must remain firmly anchored in the UN Charter and international law. We reaffirm the right of peoples to permanent sovereignty over their natural wealth and resources, as enshrined in General Assembly Resolution 1803. International cooperation should strengthen national capacities while fully respecting national ownership and development priorities. Any further normative approaches should complement existing international and regional mechanisms and emerge through an inclusive and member-state-driven process. At the same time, the Security Council has an important role in situations where the illicit exploitation of natural resources fuels armed conflict and threatens international peace and security. Existing Council tools, including sanctions, sanctions regimes, and monitoring mechanisms, should be used effectively effectively and in accordance with their mandates to disrupt the financing of armed groups. And President, the objective should not only be to secure supply chains, but ensuring that natural resources generate shared prosperity for the countries and communities that possess them. Pakistan remains committed to advancing balanced, inclusive, and consensus-based based approaches that promote sustainable development, peace, and shared prosperity. I thank you.
I thank Pakistan, and I give the floor to Latvia, now followed by Colombia and Bahrain.

Thank you very much, Excellency. First of all, I wish to Welcome the choice of the Democratic Republic of the Congo to shed light on the relevant issue of natural resources and peace today at this meeting. I also wish to thank Her Excellency Thérèse Kayekwambe Wagner, State Minister, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the DRC. Thank you for honoring us this morning with your presence.

Thank you for your presentations. Indeed, instead of lifting communities up, in many parts of the world, abundance of natural resources is linked to conflict, human rights abuses, and environmental degradation. Over the years, various standards, due diligence guidance, certification mechanisms, and transparency initiatives have proliferated to reconcile the growing resource demand and commitments to to peace, sustainable development, and responsible business conduct. This fragmentation is reflective of the wide spectrum of challenges, the actors involved— state authorities, private sector, civil society— and the properties of the natural resources themselves. And to address this, we should promote coherence, harmonization, and interoperability. So, Madam President, allow me to make 3 points on the question of the normative gaps. First, the Security Council on many occasions has recognized the link between natural resources and conflict and has taken steps to address it. For instance, by imposing targeted sanctions, including embargoes, and by mandating the development of recommendations for due diligence. Diamond and timber embargo in Liberia in the early 2000s is often cited as a positive example. It facilitated return to stability and shored up governance of natural resources in Liberia, including through the Kimberley Process. In the past, the Council has also requested a group of experts on DRC to develop recommendations on guidelines for due diligence for importers, processing industries, and consumers. Consumers of Congolese mineral products. This exemplifies that the Council can help establish and promote not mere restrictions but also soft norms. The Council should continue to deploy these tools and practices when necessary and appropriate, remaining mindful that success is highly dependent on their design, adaptability, and enforcement. This brings me to my second point, Effective measures by the Security Council require mechanisms to monitor their implementation, analyze developments, and recommend adjustments. In the case of targeted sanctions, the role of expert groups is indispensable. Experts are the Council's eyes and ears on the ground and should receive the necessary support, most importantly from the respective sanctions committees. Currently, that support is curtailed by prolonged stalemate on the allocation of subsidiary bodies chairs due to objections by one Council member. So action on expert recommendations is delayed and field missions don't take place. Engagement with neighboring and interested countries is limited and new initiatives cannot gain ground. This means that in sanctions regimes where illicit exploitation and trade of natural resources is a serious matter, of concern, work is paralyzed. So on our part, we're not averse to the idea of new instruments. We believe that priority should be given to making sure that the existing tools are in working order and can be fully utilized. Madam President, in my third and final point, I want to come back to responsible management of natural resources and supply chains. In the context of a growing global competition, The Secretary-General's Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals identified 7 voluntary guiding principles, building on existing norms, commitments, and legal obligations. These include placing human rights at the core, safeguarding environment, benefit sharing, transparency, accountability, and anti-corruption measures to ensure good governance. Indeed, whether standards, guidance, and principles that already exist, focus should be on implementation and enforcement, requiring reinvigorated political commitment and will, as well as multi-stakeholder and international cooperation. In discharging its responsibilities towards maintenance of international peace and security, this Council must also play its part to ensure that natural resources don't fuel conflict but support peace and sustainable development. And we look forward to continuing this important discussion next week at the open debate. And thank you.
I thank Latvia, and I give the floor now to Colombia, followed by Bahrain and Denmark.

Your Excellency, Ms. Teresa Calleja Guambel Wagner, State Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs. Madam Minister, Colombia thanks you for convening this meeting and recognizes the relevance of opening up discussions on the relationship between governance of national natural resources, conflict prevention, climate action, and peacebuilding. For my country, this discussion must be part of a broader context to advance towards peace with nature. This involves placing the development needs and expectations of communities at the center. Whilst making progress with the strengthening of the regulation and monitoring of supply chains with environmental and human rights safeguards. In this context, the regulatory framework is essential in order to prevent the financing of transnational organized crime and the financing of armed actors that benefit from illicit economies whilst ensuring that the legal and sustainable exploitation of natural resources leads to an improvement in the quality of life of communities and also the conservation of ecosystems, reducing the factors of vulnerability that can entrench conflicts. This is all the more relevant in a context of climate crisis, where the degradation and overexploitation of natural resources entrench vulnerabilities— the vulnerabilities of communities, the civilian populations, and of the regions they come from and can exacerbate conflict dynamics. Nevertheless, having said that, we see before us a fragmented, heterogeneous, and barely coordinated international architecture. Colombia believes that it is necessary to move towards a more coherent international regulatory framework to complement existing instruments and that strengthens international cooperation to prevent and combat the crimes that affect the environment. In this regard, Colombia supports the development of an additional protocol to the Palermo Convention geared towards strengthening the operational efficacy and legal coherence in response to these forms of transnational organized crime. This framework must reconcile peace, security, transparency, and sustainable development, but at the same time, it should comprehensively include social and environmental justice climate resilience, the protection of biodiversity, and human rights safeguards. Furthermore, it's necessary to ensure a more equitable distribution of the value and income from natural resources in order to benefit the countries that produce them, indigenous peoples, persons of African descent, and local communities. Both the standards that already exist as well as the ones that we can build collectively must be tools to drive and boost the prosperity and dignity of these communities and regions. When we see an increase in the rules of the game without them being properly coordinated, We can see an increase in costs, processes becoming more complex, and producers that have less agency being excluded. That's why harmonizing these must be grounded in shared responsibility alongside technical assistance, the strengthening of institutions with financial backing and technology transfer. In this way, traceability and transparency will be means of promoting more sustainable and inclusive development without leading to disproportionate burdens for those that participate legitimately in supply chains. It's also essential to underscore the responsibility of purchasers, merchants, and other actors in the supply chain who must vouch for the lawful, traceable, and verifiable origin of the raw materials that they acquire. Governance over natural resources must not only be the responsibility of producer countries, This must be based on true share of responsibility. Those who continue to mainly benefit from the trade of these resources must fully assume their due diligence duties, as well as transparency and accountability. This is the only way that it will be possible to ensure that international markets continue to absorb resources. This is rather the only way that it will be possible to prevent the international markets continuing to absorb resources linked to illegality, violence, and environmental damage, and ensuring that traceability is not only a formal requirement but also an effective tool that brings peace, sustainable development, and promotes a fairer distribution of value. Thank you very much.
I thank Colombia, and I now give the floor to Bahrain, who will be followed by Denmark.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, please allow me to welcome Her Excellency Minister Wagner, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the DRC. Please allow me to extend my thanks to the DRC for convening this important meeting to discuss normative gap regarding natural resources and peace and international peace and security. I would like to thank the briefers for their briefings. This discussion is of paramount importance because natural resources impact international peace and security. International experiences show that they— that 40% of internal conflicts in the past 6 decades were linked to natural resources. With the growing demand for critical minerals, We need accountability and international cooperation to promote security and stability. In this context, I would like to make the following 3 points. One, our discussion today comes at a time when the management of natural resources is of paramount importance. Despite international efforts, including a series of sanctions regimes imposed by the Security Council, But these efforts remain fragmented and are not— and do not lead to a comprehensive and coherent framework. This fragmentation leads to a duplication of frameworks that address specific resources or specific issues. As a result, the existing gaps are being exploited and natural resources are subject to illicit exploitation, which threatens the sustainability of natural resources and fuels instability within countries and across borders. The Kingdom of Bahrain reiterates that natural resources are a pillar to support economies and to strengthen strategic sectors, including agricultural inputs and food, which are a basis for global food security. Ensuring the security will not only ensure that they are not illegally exploited, but will also secure the transit waterways. These transit, such as the Hormuz, is essential to ensure that these goods reach international market. This is why we should strengthen international cooperation to protect natural resources and vital waterways and to ensure that they are secured from threats that threaten international trade. Second, Supply chains of mineral resources are being increasingly penetrated by criminal organized networks and by terrorist groups. These groups benefit from weak monitoring and regulatory gaps. This penetration and infiltration weaken governance and lead to international market disruption. This is why we underscore the importance of strengthening monitoring and cooperation frameworks for effective monitoring mechanisms. We must also strengthen financial accountability and monitoring. We must also leverage existing international frameworks to ensure that natural resources are not exploited by these groups and networks. In conclusion, it's important for any international framework to strengthen transparency and the official management and responsible governance of natural resources. Resources in full respect of state sovereignty over natural resources. In addition, this framework must be inclusive and flexible in order to take into account the different national priorities and circumstances. It must be grounded into a multi-stakeholder international cooperation. In conclusion, the responsible management of natural resources grounded in cooperation, transparency, and respect of state sovereignty is essential to support international peace and security. Natural resources must remain a driver of sustainable development and stability and must not be a driver of instability and conflict. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank Bahrain and I now give the floor to Denmark.

To the presidency of DRC for convening this important meeting. Also, a special thank you and welcome to Her Excellency Foreign Minister Wagner for being here with us today, and to our briefers for their enlightening presentations. As we've heard today, as demand for critical minerals rises in the context of, in particular, the energy transition, it is essential that natural resources become drivers of peace and development rather than sources of violence, instability, and exclusion. And on that, I would like to make 3 points. First, competition over natural resources has direct and devastating consequences for civilians. In many conflict-affected settings, the illicit exploitation and trafficking of minerals, gold, timber, and other resources finance armed groups, fuel corruption, and prolong cycles of violence by removing incentives for conflict parties to pursue political solutions. We see this, as we've heard today, in the Great Lakes region, the Sudan, in West Africa, but also in Latin America and beyond. Control over mines, transport routes, and trading hubs often translates into control over populations. Where revenues from natural resource exploitation fuel cycles of armed conflicts, civilians are displaced, livelihoods are destroyed, and access to land and basic services is undermined. I want to particularly highlight here that women and girls are particularly exposed to rape, sexual exploitation, and abuse at mining sites and along trafficking routes. Illicit trafficking, armed group financing, and sexual violence are therefore part of the same political economy of conflict, making civilian protection central to any effective response. Second, there is a clear need, as we also heard several times this morning, for better implementation and coordination of the increasingly complex set of existing frameworks. The international community already has important tools at its disposal, such as the Kimberley Process, the Great Lakes Regional Certification Mechanism, the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, and OECD's Due Diligence guidance. And the Security Council also has many tools at its disposal, from sanctions regimes, panels of experts, and reporting mandates, to peace operations. The Council can strengthen monitoring of trafficking networks and expose links between illicit resource flows and armed groups. The challenge is, of course, that these instruments remain fragmented, unevenly implemented, and often burdensome for producing countries. So the priority should be to make more systematic use of these existing tools while improving coordination with regional organizations and relevant due diligence and traceability mechanisms. Technical assistance, capacity building, and support for local producers are also necessary to facilitate responsible market access. Denmark is a firm supporter of the call of the Secretary-General for strengthened international Corporation to address this issue and has offered our support to the establishment of the Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals. Third and finally, countries rich in natural resources must be the first to benefit from them. Natural health cannot continue to generate insecurity locally while most value is captured elsewhere. A more coherent approach must promote fair revenue sharing, transparency, good governance, local value addition, job creation, and tangible benefits for affected communities. If natural resources are to support lasting peace, they must contribute not only to global supply chains but also to the prosperity, sovereignty, and development of producing states and local populations themselves.

I thank you.

Thank you.

Sir, you have the floor.

In the course of the further discussion, it will be important to build on existing mechanisms and avoid the duplication of effort. A gradual, consensus-based approach focused on practical solutions could be the most realistic way to create a comprehensive framework linking natural resources, peace, security, and sustainable

I now give the floor to Her Excellency Ana Isabel Xavier, Deputy Minister for Foreign Affairs of Portugal.

Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Madam President, allow me to start by thanking the DRC for organizing this important Agri-Forum meeting. For Portugal, an ocean-driven country, natural resources, whether they be electricity-generating fuels, critical minerals, precious metals, rare earths, biotic materials, or organic matter, underpin every aspect of daily life. From the water we drink to the cotton we wear, from the timber and iron we build with, with, to the lithium and cobalt in our batteries, natural resources are key drivers of prosperity and well-being. If well governed, if responsibly extracted and used, if the revenues from their trade are equitably shared and benefit local communities, natural resources can contribute to achieve sustainable development and the 2030 Agenda. But competition for resources has also historically resulted in social tensions and conflicts. Today, the increased scarcity of certain resources as a result of climate change and desertification of the Strip, increasing demand due to population growth, or the needs of the green and digital transitions only exacerbates resources competition. Fragile governance and lack of state capacity further complicate the scenario, opening the door to illicit exploitation and trafficking conducted by armed groups or criminal networks. The transnational nature of such threats means that we require multilateral responses and better cooperation. Their impact on international security and conflict resolution means that the Security Council cannot shy away from addressing this topic. Yet, the Security Council does not need to replace or duplicate efforts already being conducted within the United Nations, whether it be the work on environmental peacebuilding at the PBC, on conflict diamonds by the Kimberley Process, or the equity principles laid out by the Secretary-General's Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals. The Council doesn't have to replace either regional or sector-specific instruments, whether binding or voluntary. On areas such as resource governance, due diligence and traceability, or conflict financing prevention. While there remains work to be done on reducing compliance costs and administrative complexity, these different instruments forge an important institutional tapestry with mutual synergies. The Council can, however, better integrate the issue of natural resources into its work. Acknowledging their role and impact in specific situations, incorporating the issue in the reporting obligations of peacekeeping missions, or adequately updating relevant sanction regimes or embargoes would be 3 practical and tangible steps to making concrete progress in this area. As an incoming member of the Security Council, Portugal is available to work with all partners on ways to implement practical steps towards preventing and putting an end to conflicts connected to the competition for natural resources. I thank you.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency. Maintenant, je donne la parole.

And I now give the floor to the European Union, to be followed by Zimbabwe.

Thank you, President, and allow me as well to express my appreciation for the presence of Her Excellency the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Madam Magnar, in this important meeting. I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the EU and its member states. The candidate countries North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Georgia, as well as Armenia, align themselves with this statement. Chair, the EU welcomes the initiative to reflect upon the link between natural resources, peace and security, and human rights— an important yet often overlooked connection. Critical raw materials are indispensable for energy transition, digital transformation, and economic resilience. Rather than sources of instability or conflict, they should become drivers of sustainable development and shared prosperity. The EU recognizes that the current landscape of international standards and initiatives has become increasingly complex. Greater coherence, interoperability, and support for implementation can help reduce unnecessary burdens while maintaining high standards of transparency, traceability, and responsible business conduct. At the same time, any future international framework should build upon existing internationally recognized instruments and avoid creating duplicative or competing reporting and due diligence requirements. The European Union is strongly committed to preventing international trade in conflict minerals from intensifying or perpetuating conflicts and associated human rights violations and abuses. And we are doing so in line with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights. The EU Conflict Minerals Regulation was adopted in 2017. And its operational requirements applied since 2021. The aims of the regulation are to stop profits from trading conflict minerals being used to fund armed conflicts and at the same time to make responsible sourcing from conflict-affected and high-risk areas possible. We are convinced, Mr. Chair, that partnerships should also ensure that producing countries derive greater value from their natural resources, including through local value addition, investment, capacity building and skills development. This is the approach underpinning the EU Raw Materials Partnership with partner countries and translated into concrete Global Gateway investments, including the Lobito Corridor. Let me further highlight one aspect particularly relevant for peace and security. Conflict diamonds have played a major role in funding some of the most devastating civil wars in Africa. We have come a long way since the Kimberley Process was established, which has had valuable impact in improving the lives of people dependent on the trade of diamonds. From the very creation of the Kimberley Process, the EU has been committed to ensuring that it continues to fulfill its core mandate of breaking the link between diamonds and conflict. The EU has funded around €10 million in projects aimed to reinforce governance in the diamond sector and the development of alternative livelihoods. So in closing, Chair, the EU supports the Council's focus on this important issue and we are looking forward to the open debate next week. Thank you.
I thank the European Union and give the floor to Zimbabwe to be followed by Ukraine.

Thank you, Chair. We thank Her Excellency Ms. Therese Kwayikwamba Wegener, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for her presence today and delivering the opening remarks. We also thank all the briefers. Zimbabwe extends its sincere appreciation to the Democratic Republic of the Congo for convening this important Area Formula meeting on the relationship between natural resources and peace.
